title: I Used to Think Private Schools Shouldn’t Exist
author: Chad Aldeman
summary: Chad Aldeman traces how he moved from a teenage conviction that private schools should not exist to a pluralistic view of public education. He takes on Hamilton Nolan's argument that elite exit degrades public services, first by reworking Nolan's fire-safety metaphor to include standards, tests, and a fire escape. Aldeman then recounts the experiences that changed his mind: charter school research and lotteries, the limits of parent voice in a 180,000-student district that taught his own children with a debunked reading program, and Nikole Hannah-Jones's admission that even she could not change her daughter's school. He argues that abolishing private schools would not end school choice but would bundle it into the housing market. Drawing on Ashley Rogers Berner's work, he proposes a model common in other developed countries in which government sets standards, measures results, and funds a variety of school types.
points: Aldeman recasts Nolan's fire metaphor so that standards are sprinklers, tests are alarms, and school choice is the fire escape.
Research on Florida's private school choice program found that public schools facing more competition improved student achievement.
Even well-educated, policy-savvy parents like Aldeman could not realistically change a large district's reading curriculum in time for their own children.
Without private schools, choice would persist but be rationed by the price of a house.
He favors a pluralistic system with common academic standards and tests but freedom for Montessori, STEM, classical, and other models.
quotes: Back when I was a righteous teenager, I didn’t think private schools should exist. I thought that if all kids had to go to public schools everyone would work to make them better.

In this metaphor, the sprinkler system is a set of standards for public schools. The fire alarms are standardized tests so we know when something is wrong. And the fire escape is the option that anyone can leave at anytime whenever they start to smell smoke.

It was amazing to see the hope and promise of the (mostly Black and Hispanic) parents who desperately wanted to get their child into this school. It was also crushing to realize that the stakes were so high because there wasn’t space for all of them.

Large school systems are complicated institutions with competing constituencies, entrenched practices, and their own ideas about what good education looks like. Keeping dissatisfied families inside the system does not necessarily turn their dissatisfaction into better schools.
But getting rid of private schools wouldn’t eliminate school choice. It would just preserve a version in which access to the most desirable schools is bundled with the price of a house.
It turns out that most other places in the developed world fund a broad array of school types. Their public education systems aren’t bundled into the housing market.
We don't all have to want the same thing for our kids, but don’t yuck my yum, and I promise not to interfere with yours.
